# Model evaluation report

*Generated by `python -m src.evaluate`. Every number below is computed from the saved model and data -
nothing is typed in by hand. Re-running with different library versions may change values slightly.*

## 1. Setup
- Dataset: IBM Telco Customer Churn sample dataset; development set n = 5634, held-out test n = 1409.
- Test prevalence of churn: 26.5%.
- **Final model:** `LightGBM` with feature set `base`.
  Selection rule: highest CV PR-AUC (LightGBM, 0.6729); within 1 SE (0.0101) -> ['LightGBM', 'XGBoost']; simplest chosen -> LightGBM
- **Decision threshold:** 0.22, chosen by the rule "minimise expected cost on out-of-fold development predictions" - i.e. on out-of-fold development predictions, minimising expected
  cost under *illustrative* assumptions. It was fixed before the test set was scored.

## 3. Held-out test results (scored once)
| Metric | Final model @ chosen threshold | Final model @ 0.50 | Dummy baseline @ 0.50 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Accuracy | 0.723 | 0.801 | 0.735 |
| Precision | 0.487 | 0.660 | 0.000 |
| Recall | 0.832 | 0.519 | 0.000 |
| F1 | 0.615 | 0.581 | 0.000 |
| Share of customers flagged | 45.3% | 20.9% | 0.0% |
| ROC-AUC (threshold-free) | 0.849 | 0.849 | 0.500 |
| PR-AUC / Average precision (threshold-free) | 0.665 | 0.665 | 0.265 |
| Brier score (lower is better) | 0.135 | 0.135 | 0.195 |

Confusion matrix at the chosen threshold: TP = 311, FP = 327, TN = 708, FN = 63.

**Uncertainty (bootstrap over the 1409 test customers):**
- ROC-AUC: 0.849 (95% CI 0.827 to 0.870)
- PR-AUC: 0.665 (95% CI 0.612 to 0.713)
- Precision @ threshold: 48.7% (95% CI 44.8% to 52.5%)
- Recall @ threshold: 83.2% (95% CI 79.1% to 86.7%)
- Brier: 0.135 (95% CI 0.124 to 0.144)

Consistency check: the out-of-fold development PR-AUC (0.670) lies inside the test-set 95% interval, i.e. the test result is consistent with the cross-validation estimate.

Reminder: the dummy baseline's accuracy of 73.5% comes from always predicting "stays" - this is why accuracy alone is misleading here.

## 4. Threshold analysis (ILLUSTRATIVE costs - assumptions, not measurements)
Assumed: customer value V = $400; intervention cost C = $25 per flagged customer;
intervention success probability s = 30%.
If probabilities were perfectly calibrated the break-even rule is *flag if p > C/(sV)* = 0.21.

On the held-out test set, at the pre-chosen threshold 0.22, the framework gives an expected net saving of
**$21,370** ($15,167 per 1,000 customers) versus doing nothing,
compared with $11,306 per 1,000 at the default 0.50 threshold and
$6,852 per 1,000 for flagging everyone.
These are model-based expectations under assumed costs; they are **not** measured retention gains.

On the development (out-of-fold) data, every threshold from 0.15 to 0.26 gives expected savings within 2% of the best - the cost curve is flat near its optimum, so the exact threshold matters much less than choosing a sensible region and getting the costs right.

Test-set metrics across thresholds (descriptive only - not used for selection):

| threshold | flagged_pct | precision | recall | f1 | tp | fp | tn | fn | net_savings_per_1000 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.100 | 60.823 | 0.412 | 0.944 | 0.574 | 353 | 504 | 531 | 21 | 14858.055 |
| 0.200 | 47.126 | 0.477 | 0.848 | 0.611 | 317 | 347 | 688 | 57 | 15216.466 |
| 0.300 | 37.686 | 0.537 | 0.762 | 0.630 | 285 | 246 | 789 | 89 | 14850.958 |
| 0.400 | 29.312 | 0.600 | 0.663 | 0.630 | 248 | 165 | 870 | 126 | 13793.471 |
| 0.500 | 20.866 | 0.660 | 0.519 | 0.581 | 194 | 100 | 935 | 180 | 11305.891 |

Threshold choice changes *decisions* (who is flagged); it does not change the model's ranking of customers, so ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are identical for every threshold.

**gender**

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Female | 687 | 0.281 | 0.453 | 0.505 | 0.813 | 0.266 | 0.845 |
| Male | 722 | 0.251 | 0.453 | 0.471 | 0.851 | 0.267 | 0.854 |

**SeniorCitizen**

| SeniorCitizen | n | churn_rate | flagged_rate | precision | recall | mean_predicted_prob | roc_auc |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| No | 1187 | 0.233 | 0.400 | 0.459 | 0.790 | 0.239 | 0.850 |
| Yes | 222 | 0.441 | 0.734 | 0.571 | 0.949 | 0.413 | 0.785 |

Groups differ in base churn rate, so differing flag rates are expected; compare precision/recall and look for large gaps.
Small groups give noisy estimates. Using attributes such as gender or age to decide who receives retention offers raises fairness and
legal questions that should be reviewed before any real deployment.

## 6. Limitations
- Single random split of one snapshot dataset: no temporal validation, no check for drift.
- Dataset is an IBM *sample* (fictional telecom) - results do not transfer to a real operator.
- Churn labels are observational; associations (here and in SHAP) are not causal effects of interventions.
- Cost figures are illustrative; real value, cost and success rates must be measured (ideally with an A/B test).
- Test metrics have sampling uncertainty (see confidence intervals); small differences between models are not meaningful.
